stars.text: BORI Bhīṣmaparvan 6.2.31 describes Arundhatī in front of Vasiṣṭha among Vyāsa’s omens. This is an editorial paraphrase. Oak’s 2016 diagrams interpret it as crossing the meridian first.
stars.method: Compare upper transit times of Alcor (HIP 65477) and Mizar A (HIP 65378), with component, proper motion, long-term precession, time scale and uncertainty recorded. The Greenwich modern comparison ran. Historical boundaries are awaiting independent review.
stars.dependencies: The stellar test shares the precession premise with the seasonal argument. The stated intervals are model-dependent constraints.

season.text: BORI 6.114 narrates Bhīṣma’s fall. At 13.153.6 and 27–28 the sun has turned north, and Bhīṣma names fifty-eight nights and the month Māgha. Editorial paraphrase.
season.method: Identify the start and end of the nights and the month convention. Compute the northern solar turning point and lunar phase under each combination. The full comparison awaits implementation.
season.dependencies: Shares calendar definitions with the war-month clue. Oak’s narrower combined inference from items 2–4 is dependent on both inputs.

moon.text: Oak’s public noon table for Kurukṣetra describes his candidate, from new Moon on day 1 to full Moon on day 15 and the waning half by day 18. Matching his table to individual CE passages remains open.
moon.method: At a defined time each day compare the Moon’s longitude relative to the Sun, its nakṣatra, and the adopted lunar month convention. Check the precession and seasonal rule behind the approximate threshold. The modern Moon lesson has calculated examples.
moon.dependencies: The threshold uses the same seasons and lunar calendar as the Bhīṣma argument. Comparing the candidate’s moon phases requires the same proposed opening day.

planets.text: BORI 6.43.38 compares warriors to Mars and Mercury, while 6.43.54 compares a fight to Venus and Mars. Oak’s item 1 describes Venus and Mercury, a discrepancy to resolve before testing. His item 2 reports about 3–7° between Venus and Mars for his war interval.
planets.method: Verify the Sanskrit object identifications and whether the comparison describes an observation. Define separation, epoch, visibility, and a tolerance before searching. The 2019 post credits Saiswaroopa Iyer for new leads. No historical planetary checks ran here.
planets.dependencies: The reported comparisons use the proposed war days and site. Bhīṣma 6.2–3 also supplies other omen records.

eclipse.text: Oak discusses a coppery Kārttika Moon in BORI 6.2.23 and solar and lunar obscuration in 6.3.28–29. He gives 16 and 30 October 5561 BCE as a candidate pair, counting 13 days between the two dates and leaving the omen’s assignment to the first day open. The darkness at Jayadratha’s death in BORI 7.121 belongs to a separate narrative setting. Ganguli’s translation credits Kṛṣṇa’s yoga.
eclipse.method: Test syzygy, lunar node distance, contact geometry and horizon at the proposed site. A long-term Earth-rotation model controls where a solar shadow might cross. No historical eclipse or local visibility check ran here.
eclipse.dependencies: Uses the same lunar ephemeris and candidate times as the lunar clue. The Jayadratha scene carries its own textual assumption.
links: Oak’s response on eclipses and day counting

dwarka.text: BORI 16.8.40 narrates the inundation. Oak’s 2020 summary item 10 gives 5525 BCE for the flooding he proposes.
dwarka.method: Rao’s 1987 survey compared recovered structures, pottery and anchors to known assemblages. It proposed 1400–1300 BCE for particular Lustrous Red Ware by ceramic comparison, with limited old organic material for direct dating. The proposal dates pottery. Connecting it to a particular inundation requires a securely dated depositional horizon.
dwarka.dependencies: Oak’s summary treats this as corroboration. The atlas has no source-backed link that converts the marine material into a numerical war-date constraint.

track.label: Dwarka and Bet Dwarka ceramic comparison · approx. 1400–1300 BCE

rakhigarhi.text: Shinde et al. (Cell, 2019), sample I6113 from the Rakhigarhi cemetery. The paper analysed one genome after screening 61 individuals and compared its ancestry to other ancient populations.
rakhigarhi.method: The laboratory extracted and sequenced ancient DNA for ancestry analysis. Collagen preservation prevented direct radiocarbon dating of the burial. The reported 2800–2300 BCE context comes from seven radiocarbon dates on charcoal from the habitation area. The burial’s absolute age remains uncertain.
rakhigarhi.dependencies: Oak lists genetics as corroboration in his project summary. A paper, passage, or specimen association stating how I6113 would date the war has yet to be identified.

population.text: Narasimhan et al. (Science, 2019) compared genome-wide data from 523 ancient individuals in South and Central Asian contexts over roughly the last 8,000 years.
population.method: The team used dated assemblages and individual sample contexts, then modelled shared ancestry and mixture. Limits vary by sample location, radiocarbon coverage and the sampled populations that stand in for past groups.
population.dependencies: The population model supplies context for comparisons with Harappan ancestry. The atlas has yet to locate a source linking a specific sample in this study to a specific war event.

track.label: Ancient-DNA sampling scope · approximately the past 8,000 years

rivers.text: Singh et al. (Nature Communications, 2017) tested how the Ghaggar–Hakra palaeochannel relates to former Sutlej flow and to urban settlements of the Indus civilisation.
rivers.method: The team used sediment provenance and optically stimulated luminescence to date deposits. They report that the Sutlej began abandoning that valley after about 15,000 years ago and completed the shift shortly after about 8,000 years ago. The history of the channel leaves the epic river’s identity and remembered times open.
rivers.dependencies: Oak’s project summary names hydrology generally. It gives no testable match to this particular channel deposit or to the date of a named battle.

track.label: Approximate Sutlej channel abandonment sequence · 15,000–8,000 years ago

hastinapura.text: B. B. Lal’s excavation report identifies Period II at Hastināpura by Painted Grey Ware and discusses an erosion or flood horizon and a subsequent break in occupation.
hastinapura.method: The excavation used stratigraphy and comparison of ceramic assemblages. Lal’s Table I puts Period II at approximately 1100–800 BCE. An independent absolute date for the layer and a link to a narrated person or event would be needed to make it a war-date test.
hastinapura.dependencies: This context is linked to the map’s modern site. Oak’s specific use of the excavation and its proposed historical associations still needs a cited edition and page.

track.label: Hastināpura Period II · Lal’s approx. 1100–800 BCE

candidate.text: In his 2015 calendar note Oak specifies 16 October 5561 BCE as proleptic Julian. The atlas consulted his public posts and linked book overview. Precise page and figure references for the full 2011 book await an accessible copy.
candidate.method: Translate the labelled calendar date to the time scale of each independent test, then compare the candidate with the remaining ranges and unfiltered observations. Passing the displayed broad bounds leaves many other years possible.
candidate.dependencies: The public day-by-day lunar and planetary checks use this starting day. The local prereview transit run is a separate comparison and still awaits independent review.
